newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Market eagerly awaits Philippines 20-yr bond debut.
newsitem.headline: Market eagerly awaits Philippines 20-yr bond debut.

text.p: Next week's debut 20-year fixed rate Philippine Treasury bond is expected to get a warm welcome especially from institutional investors, traders and officials said on Friday.

"I believe the issue will be very well-received," Cesar Santos, president of the Money Market Association of the Philippines, told Reuters. Santos is also vice president for treasury of Citibank NA in Manila.
Some traders expect oversubscription to push the coupon for Tuesday's two-billion peso offering to as low as 14.0 percent.
The last 10-year fixed-rate bond, offered in late January, fetched a coupon of 14.125 percent. The bond is currently being traded between 12.75 percent to 13.5 percent.
"I might be a little aggressive, but I think there will be great demand for that issue," a trader at one of the leading investment houses said.
He said the firm had received a lot of interest on the issue especially from pension fund and retirement fund managers.
The 20-year T-bond will be the longest maturing locally-denominated government secury in southeast Asia.
The Philippine government is lengthening the tenor of its domestic debt as investors gain more confidence over its long-term economic prospects.

Santos said the issue will be used as a benchmark for long term domestic corporate borrowings. At present, corporations borrow long-term pesos based on the three-month T-bill rate which is re-priced every quarter.
Philippine Treasurer Caridad Valdehuesa said insurance companies and foreign institutional investors have been pressing her to double the issue to four billion pesos.

"Now that we have liberalised the financial industry, there are more players in the markets, such as thrift banks, savings and mortgage banks, development banks, and insurance companies. There is a greater demand for longer-term assets," she said.
"This provides the market with an additional menu of investment instruments," she added.
The Philippines offers three-, six- and twelve-month Treasury bills every week, two-year bonds every month, and five-, seven- and ten-year bonds each quarter.

Ayen Guevara, vice president for treasury of leading life insurer Philippine American Life Insurance Co Inc, said insurance companies would especially find the 20-year bond useful since it can be matched against its long-term liabilities.
"In the past, we were constrained to use short-term assets to match our long-term premiums," she said.

However, some traders expressed reservations on whether the strong appetite can be sustained in future auctions as the possible lack of liquidity in the secondary market might turn off some securities dealers.

"We are talking here about the buy-and-hold type of investors. If the demand has been satisfied, no bank would like to hold on to that type of instrument for that long," a trader from a foreign bank said.
However, Treasurer Valdehuesa noted the same fears had been raised before the maiden offerings of the two-, five-, seven- and ten-year bonds.
"These are the prophets of doom. But as you can see, they still come back to us every auction," she said.
